To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the attitudes of cancer patients, their family caregivers, oncologist and members of the public toward critical interventions administered at end of life were different, but that all groups were in agreement about the withdrawal of futile treatment and the use active pain control, and were opposed to the active ending of the patient's life.

cancer patients, family carers, oncologists, and members of the public had a similar attitude towards futile and ameliorate end of life care, but oncologists had a less positive attitude towards active euthanasia.

a large majority of cancer patients, their family caregivers, oncologist and members of the Korean general population support the withdrawal of futile treatments and the practice of pain control, but that oncologists are much less likely to support active euthanasia than the other groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ethical issues surrounding critical end-of-life care, including euthanasia.
attitudes toward the end of life, not the end of life itself.
the ethical issues of end-of-life care, which are relevant to both the general public and medical professionals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
most of those surveyed in our study supported the withdrawal of futile treatments and the use of palliative measures to control pain.

a large majority of cancer patients, oncologists, family caregivers and members of the Korean general population support withdrawal of futile life support and active pain control, whereas a majority of cancer patients and members of the public but a minority of family caregivers and oncologists support withholding of life-sus-taining treatment.
the general population and cancer patients are more likely to accept euthanasia than oncologists and family caregivers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the majority of Korean patients, family caregivers and the general public support the withdrawal of futile treatment and the use active pain control at the end of the life of a terminally ill patient; however, the majority of patients and the general public do not support withholding of life-sustainment, whereas the majority of family caregivers and oncologists do.
most of the participants supported active pain control and withholding of life-sus-taining measures, whereas a minority supported the active ending of a patient's life.

a significant majority of Korean cancer patients, family members, oncologists and the general public approved the withdrawal of futile treatment and the use and withholding of active pain control at the end of the life of terminally-ill patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the attitudes of cancer patients and their caregivers toward end-of-life care should be carefully considered in the design of health policies.
there is a wide gap in attitudes among the four groups toward the active termination of life.
there is a need to educate oncologists about the need for and the importance of euthanasia and other critical interventions at the ends of life.
